instructions: Score each item with quality-rubric.md. input, when present, is the problem the item's tree answers; chain lists the reasons above it, from the top; siblings are the other reasons answering the same why.

items.input: Our nightly database backup job silently skips some runs, and nobody notices until a restore is needed.
items.question: why
chain: A stale lock from an overrunning or crashed previous run makes the next night's job exit cleanly with success, skipping the backup.
The lockfile has no expiry or liveness check, so a crashed run's lock persists until someone deletes it by hand.
items.reason: The script tests only whether the lockfile exists, never whether the PID written inside it is still running.
siblings: Lock removal lives in an EXIT trap, which never runs when the dump is SIGKILLed by the OOM killer or the host reboots.
The lockfile sits on persistent disk rather than tmpfs under /run, so even a reboot does not clear it.

items.input: Our nightly database backup job silently skips some runs, and nobody notices until a restore is needed.
items.question: why
chain: No scheduled restore drill or check for tonight's backup file exists, so missing backups are first discovered during a real restore.
items.reason: No team owns the backup's outcome; the cron script was added by one engineer and never assigned to an on-call rotation.
siblings: Backup success was defined as the cron job completing, so nobody set a recovery objective requiring proof that tonight's file is restorable.
A full restore drill is costly, needing a spare database host and hours of runtime, so it was judged not worth automating.

items.input: Our nightly database backup job silently skips some runs, and nobody notices until a restore is needed.
items.question: why
chain: Alerting fires only on a failed exit code, so a run that never starts or exits early emits no signal at all.
The alert is an on-failure trap inside the backup wrapper script, so it only fires when that script runs and errors.
items.reason: Guard clauses for an unmounted backup target or full disk log a warning and exit 0, which the failure trap treats as success.
siblings: The backup was set up as a lone cron entry on the database host, with no orchestrator to own run state or alerting.
The monitoring stack collects host metrics only and offers no job-level check, so the script's own trap was the sole hook available.

items.input: Our nightly database backup job silently skips some runs, and nobody notices until a restore is needed.
items.question: why
chain: A stale lock from an overrunning or crashed previous run makes the next night's job exit cleanly with success, skipping the backup.
The dump step has no timeout or watchdog, so a hung run keeps holding the lock into the next night's start.
items.reason: The script dates from when dumps took minutes, and no upper bound was added as database growth stretched runtimes to hours.
siblings: The dump blocks waiting on a table lock held by a long-running transaction or migration left open overnight.
Writes to the backup share stall on an unresponsive hard-mounted NFS export, leaving the dump process blocked indefinitely.

items.input: Our nightly database backup job silently skips some runs, and nobody notices until a restore is needed.

chain: A stale lock from an overrunning or crashed previous run makes the next night's job exit cleanly with success, skipping the backup.
items.reason: The wrapper deliberately treats "lock already held" as a harmless no-op and returns exit 0, to avoid overlapping runs.
